items.question: Examine the political and social organisation of the Early Vedic (Rigvedic) period. To what extent was it tribal, participatory and egalitarian?
items.modelAnswer: Rigvedic polity was **tribal and patriarchal**. The tribe (**Jana**) was led by the **Rajan** (chief), who was not an absolute monarch but was aided and checked by two assemblies — the **Sabha**, an advisory council of elders and noblemen handling judicial and administrative matters, and the **Samiti**, a broader assembly of clan representatives that took part in the **election of the Rajan** and debated war, alliances and welfare. Authority was organised through a nested hierarchy of kin-based units: **Kula** (family, under the Kulapa) → **Grama** (village, under the Gramini) → **Visu** (group of villages, under the Vishayapati) → **Jana** (tribe, under the Rajan). Society rested on **Gotra** (lineage) and was **patriarchal**, with descent traced through the male line. The term **Varna** initially meant 'colour' and only later signified social classification; the **Purushasukta** of the 10th Mandala marks the **beginning of the fourfold division** (Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra), but caste was **not yet rigid**. Thus the period was strongly tribal and comparatively participatory (through Sabha and Samiti and the relatively respected position of women who composed hymns), yet the presence of slavery and the emergent Varna order show it was not fully egalitarian.
keyPoints: Tribal, patriarchal polity: Jana led by the Rajan, checked by Sabha (elders) and Samiti (assembly that elected the Rajan)
Nested units: Kula (Kulapa) → Grama (Gramini) → Visu (Vishayapati) → Jana (Rajan)
Society based on Gotra/lineage; Varna first meant 'colour', later social class
Purushasukta (10th Mandala) begins the fourfold Varna division; caste not yet rigid
Participatory elements (assemblies, respected women) coexist with slavery and emergent hierarchy

items.question: Discuss the economy and religion of the Rigvedic Aryans, bringing out how a pastoral economy shaped their religious life.
items.modelAnswer: The Rigvedic economy was predominantly **pastoral**, centred on **cattle rearing**, with cows so prized that battle terms such as **gavishta** and **gesu** literally meant 'searching for cows'. **Agriculture** was growing but limited: it is described extensively in the **4th Mandala**, with **barley (yava)** and **wheat** as staple crops and a rich vocabulary — **Urvara** (fertile land), **Langal** (plough), **Karishu** (manure) and **Khilya** (pasture). Exchange rested on the **barter system**, mainly of cattle, with **little evidence of external trade**. This cattle-and-nature-bound life is mirrored in **religion**, which was **polytheistic nature worship** expressed through **yajnas** (fire sacrifices). The great gods personify natural and martial forces vital to a herding-warrior people: **Indra** (thunder, rain and war) was the most important; **Agni** (fire) carried offerings to the gods; **Varuna** (called **Ritashya Gopa**) upheld cosmic order; and **Soma** (9th Mandala) was both a plant and a sacred drink. Deities were grouped by domain — **sky** (Surya, Dyaus, Varuna), **space** (Indra, Rudra, Vayu) and **earth** (Agni, Soma, Prithvi) — showing that religion sanctified the natural forces on which the pastoral economy depended.
keyPoints: Predominantly pastoral, cattle-centred economy; battle terms gavishta/gesu ('seeking cows')
Growing but limited agriculture (4th Mandala): barley and wheat; terms Urvara, Langal, Karishu, Khilya
Barter exchange dominated; little external trade
Polytheistic nature worship through yajnas; Indra (war/rain) foremost, Agni (fire), Varuna (Ritashya Gopa), Soma (9th Mandala)
Deities grouped as sky (Surya/Dyaus/Varuna), space (Indra/Rudra/Vayu), earth (Agni/Soma/Prithvi) — sanctifying nature

items.question: Assess the value of the Rigveda and allied sources for reconstructing the history of the Early Vedic period.
items.modelAnswer: The **Rigveda**, one of the world's oldest texts, composed in **Vedic Sanskrit** (c. 1500–1000 BCE) and preserved by a remarkable **oral tradition**, is the single most important source for the Early Vedic period — a value recognised by its inclusion in the **UNESCO Memory of the World Register (2007)**. Its ten Mandalas yield datable social detail: the **4th** on agriculture, the **7th** on the **Dasharajnya War** (King Sudas of the Bharatas on the Parusni/Ravi), the **9th** on Soma, and the **10th** carrying the **Purushasukta**. It preserves vivid glimpses — a **boat with a hundred oars**, and a student's line, *'I am a poet, my father is a physician, and my mother grinds the grain.'* Beyond the Rigveda, comparative sources confirm and contextualise the Aryans: the **Avesta** of Iran (closely related Zoroastrian texts), the **Mitanni inscriptions** of Syria and **Kassite inscriptions** of Iraq that name Vedic gods (**Indra, Varuna, Mitra**). **Archaeology** adds a material check — **Painted Grey pottery**, the 13-room house at **Bhagwanpura**, fortified settlements at **Ropar** and **Sarai Hira**, metal tools and animal (horse, cattle) bones — while emerging **DNA studies** probe migration. The limitation is that the Rigveda is essentially a **religious/hymnal** text, so its picture of society is partial and idealised; combining textual, comparative and archaeological evidence gives the most reliable reconstruction.
keyPoints: Rigveda: oldest text, Vedic Sanskrit (c.1500–1000 BCE), oral tradition, UNESCO Memory of the World (2007)
Comparative sources: Avesta (Iran), Mitanni (Syria) and Kassite (Iraq) inscriptions naming Indra/Varuna/Mitra
Archaeology: Painted Grey pottery, Bhagwanpura 13-room house, forts at Ropar/Sarai Hira, metal tools, animal bones; DNA studies on migration
Limitation: Rigveda is a religious/hymnal text — a partial, idealised picture; corroborate with archaeology
